title: 20 Questions With Electronic Pioneer Suzanne Ciani: ‘Now I Have An Audience. The Kids Know What’s Going On’
summary: The 80-year-old electronic visionary performs her first show in Scotland this weekend before a festival set in Roswell, New Mexico next month.
contentText:
Suzanne Ciani was not only present at the beginning of electronic music, but helped develop the technology that would become the basis of an entire global genre. Born in Ohio, Ciani earned a master’s degree in composition at UC Berkeley, where she met synthesizer designer Don Buchla and became one of the first people to master the Buchla modular analog synthesizer.

In 1974, she founded Ciani/Musica, where she developed sounds for brands including AT&T, General Electric and Coca-Cola. (The soda’s “ pop & pour ” sound logo was her creation, as was the Columbia Pictures intro score .) She’s released more than 25 studio and live albums and received five Grammy nominations, all in the new age category. Now 80 years old, she’s experienced a late career renaissance on the power of her live modular synthesizer performances, work that’s brought her into the fray of the dance/electronic festival circuit and earned her friends like Floating Points and collaborator Kaitlyn Aurelia Smith.

This weekend, Ciani performs her first ever concert in Scotland, at Glasgow’s Sonica Festival, a longstanding art and experimental music festival where Ciani will perform among a lineup of other experimental artists from around the world. In early November, she’ll be back home in the States to play Atomika, a new science and music festival happening in the remote desert outside of Roswell, New Mexico.

Ahead of these performances, Ciani spoke to Billboard over Zoom from her home in Northern California about her life in technology.

1. Where are you in the world right now, and what’s the setting like?

I’m home for a change, because I spend a lot of time traveling. And home right now is temporary, because I am in the process of selling my house after 34 years — a house I never thought I would leave because it was so exquisitely beautiful. But I just wanted a new chapter. I wrote many albums there. I had a beautiful life there, and now I’m ready for something else. It’s healthy. It’s stimulating. The basis of technology is change. It’s built in.

2. What is the first album or piece of music that you bought for yourself, and what was the medium?

Actually my mother bought it, and it was a Rachmaninoff Piano Concerto and a Grieg Piano Concerto. It was romantic classical music. My mother had gone to a fire sale and come home with this stack of LPs, and I would just sit and listen to them morning, noon and night, swooning at the emotion of the music.

3. What did your parents do for a living when you were a kid ?

My dad was an orthopedic surgeon. My mom was a mom. She had six kids and was the consummate homemaker. She could sew anything. She could build anything. She had tools in her jewelry box.

4. What did they think of what you do for a living?

My dad was Italian. He had five daughters and one son, and his idea about women was that they were supposed to get married, have children and take care of a man, so he wasn’t that excited about my independence. I had a period where I was living in New York City and making a lot of money, and he came to visit. I had my Mercedes convertible, and to me it just seemed normal. I didn’t think of it as a statement of any kind. He said, “All you care about is money” and just deeply took it as a comment on the direction of my life. I hadn’t seen myself in that light, because I didn’t feel that way. I didn’t care about money. I did have it, but I didn’t care about it. That situation made me focus a bit more on how I projected my values and about what my lifestyle was communicating. I mean, this is complicated. You’d need a shrink to really understand this.

5. This next question feels clunky in response to what you just said : what was the first non-gear thing that you bought for yourself when you started making money as an artist?

The car. I love machines, and to me, a car was a machine. It was right up my alley. The Mercedes was a beautiful machine. I knew nothing about buying cars. I simply went into a car dealer, paid full price and drove it away. I kept it in a garage across the street. It does sound a little pretentious, but all I did was drive to the Hamptons. I immediately got a speeding ticket because I had no idea how fast I was going. You didn’t feel speed in it.

6. If you had to recommend one album for someone looking to get into electronic music, what album would you give them?

I want to say my album. I think the Buchla Concerts 1975 , even though it was really just a document. It wasn’t a finely recorded album. It came from a cassette tape during a live quadraphonic concert, but I’m so grateful that it documented the live [aspect]. What I’m interested in is the live performance. That’s where I came from. I’ve also made a lot of studio albums, but my founding love of electronic music was as a performance instrument.

7. When all of these instruments, these machines, were being created and you got your hands on them, did you know you were at the dawn of something?

I was so excited about it. My mistake was that I thought the whole world was excited too. I went out into the world with this exciting machine and ran into a wall. Nobody knew what it was, or where the sound was coming from. So the backlash of that excitement was loneliness. I was frustrated that nobody understood what was happening. I had no audience then. Now I have an audience. The kids know what’s going on. They have the machines. Nobody had them back then.

8. How did you manage that loneliness you felt?

I became a teacher. I became extremely patient. I said to myself, “You’re going to have to be responsible for this gap, and so when people ask a question, take your time, answer it. Doesn’t matter how many times you’ve answered it. Be genuinely empathic with their desire to understand, don’t lash out and say, ‘What’s wrong with you?'” I developed this kind of teaching persona that I still have today.

Another thing I did was my first album, Seven Waves , which was a combination of classical and electronic. I grew up with romantic, operatic music in my Italian family, and my Italian heritage was about emotion and melody. So when I did Seven Waves , it was this synthesis of the electronic and my classical background that people understood.

9. Do you think about your legacy and, if so, do you think this teaching aspect is part of it?

Absolutely… But a lot of my understanding of what I’ve done, or who I am, or what the legacy is, is brought to me from outside myself. I was just in it. So when people say, “She designed electronic sound and put it into television,” for me, that’s a complicated little world.

10. Yes, you were one of the first women composers in major advertising and made music for brands like Coca-Cola, AT&T and General Electric. How was it complicated?

Because we come to television with a certain prejudice that it’s some populist, cheesy thing. It wasn’t that. It was a frontier. People at record labels were looking backwards. They had their music, they had their successes, and they wanted more of that. People in advertising wanted something new. They didn’t even need to understand what it was. It was, “Just do whatever you want, as long as it’s new.” And that was technology. In technology, you woke up every day, and there was something new, and it stimulated you.

11. Was that exciting?

It was hand in hand with the the evolution of technology. Dishwashers were using chips. Elevators were using chips. There were new chips that did voices, that you could put into games. There were new ways of making images. It was the start.
